drills.title: USD/JPY short: P&L in yen and dollars
drills.question: You are short $5,000,000 of USD/JPY at 152.40 and cover at 150.90. What is the P&L in yen, and in dollars at the closing rate?
common_mistakes: Reporting the P&L in dollars directly as 5,000,000 x 1.50
Getting the sign wrong: USD/JPY fell, so a dollar short gains
drills.intuition: P&L on a BASE position is earned in the QUOTE currency; it becomes dollars only when converted at the rate prevailing when you convert it.
drills.takeaway: Always state the currency of a P&L figure and the rate used to translate it.

drills.title: Inverse-pair percentage change
drills.question: EUR/USD moves from 1.0500 to 1.1025. By what percentage did the euro change in dollars, and the dollar in euros?
drills.intuition: Percentage changes are not symmetric under inversion: 1/(1+x) - 1 is not -x.
drills.takeaway: Compute the inverse change as S0/S1 - 1.

drills.title: Forward points and the basis
drills.question: EUR/USD spot 1.0800; one-year USD 4.00%, EUR 2.00% (accrual 1.0). The market one-year forward is quoted at +235 points. Compute the CIP forward points and the implied cross-currency basis on the euro rate (bp). Who benefits from the gap: a U.S. investor hedging euro assets or a euro investor hedging dollar assets?

rubric: Market forward 1.1035 is above CIP, implying a negative basis of about -21.5 bp
A U.S. investor selling euros forward receives more dollars (benefits); a euro investor selling dollars forward pays more (loses)
Notes that the basis tends to widen at quarter-ends and in funding stress

drills.solution: F_CIP = 1.08 x 1.04/1.02 = 1.101176 (+211.8 pips). F_mkt = 1.1035. b = 1.08 x 1.04/1.1035 - 1 - 0.02 = -0.215% (-21.5 bp). Euros are rich forward: the dollar-based hedger of euro assets gains, the euro-based hedger of dollar assets pays.
common_mistakes: Reading positive points as a forecast that the euro will rise
Getting the sign of the basis backwards
Assuming the basis helps all hedgers
drills.intuition: The basis is the price of synthetic dollar funding beyond the rate differential.
drills.takeaway: Hedge cost = rate differential + basis; check live forward points, not policy rates.

drills.title: Break-even crash probability for a carry trade
drills.question: A carry trade earns 0.30% a month on notional. In a crash month the investment currency falls 9% (take the crash-month result as carry minus 9%). What monthly crash probability makes expected return zero, and at that probability, what is the chance of at least one crash in a year?

parts.label: P(at least one crash in 12 months) (%)

common_mistakes: Computing P(at least one crash) as 12p = 40% instead of 1 - (1 - p)^12
Treating a crash-free three-year record as evidence that p is below p*
drills.intuition: Carry is selling crash insurance; the premium is small and regular, the payout rare and large.
drills.takeaway: If you cannot bound p away from p*, size small or abstain.

drills.title: Cash call at the roll of a sterling hedge
drills.question: A U.S. fund hedges 60% of £20,000,000 of hotel equity with a one-year forward struck at GBP/USD 1.2600. At the roll, spot is 1.3400. Rates are USD 4.25%, GBP 4.75% (accrual 1.0). Compute the cash settlement, the new forward, and the shortfall against a $700,000 reserve.
common_mistakes: Using the full £20m rather than the hedged 60%
Getting the sign wrong: a short sterling forward loses when sterling rises
Assuming the new forward is struck at the old forward rate
drills.intuition: A rolling hedge re-strikes at spot; the loss on the old forward is paid in cash while the hotel's dollar gain stays unrealized.
drills.takeaway: Size the reserve to the hedge, or the hedge to the reserve, before the roll date.

drills.title: The peg that has never been in doubt
drills.question: A broker offers a retail center in a country whose currency has been pegged to the dollar for ten years. Local yield 12%. The one-year NDF implies a 10% forward discount on the local currency. Reserves have fallen for five months. You cannot obtain short-term external debt data before the bid deadline. T-bills yield 4.25%. Bid, bid unhedged, bid hedged, or abstain?

rubric: Computes the hedged dollar yield: 1.12/1.10 - 1 = 1.8%, below T-bills: no spread once currency risk is removed
Recognizes that an unhedged bid is a bet on the peg, and that the forward discount signals a material market-implied devaluation probability
Names the missing data (short-term external debt vs reserves, non-resident deposits) as decisive for first-generation timing
Notes the one-year NDF cannot hedge a multi-year illiquid hold and may be unavailable in a crisis
Concludes that abstaining (or bidding only at a price that prices in a large devaluation, with local debt) is the best answer under the deadline

drills.solution: Hedged yield 1.8% < 4.25% T-bill. Unhedged requires the peg to hold. The key variable is unknown and the deadline prevents learning it. Abstain, or submit a conditional bid at a much lower price that survives a large devaluation.
common_mistakes: Treating ten years of stability as evidence of low risk
Assuming the NDF can be rolled through a crisis
drills.intuition: A peg compresses observed volatility until the day it breaks.
drills.takeaway: When the decisive fact is unknowable before the deadline, abstention is a position.

drills.title: Hedging transports the spread
drills.question: A Japanese investor compares a U.S. hotel at a 7.0% cap rate (hedged to yen with one-year forwards, CIP, USD 4.25%, JPY 0.50%) with a Japanese hotel at 4.0%. Compute the hedged yen yield and the spread ratio (1+y)/(1+r) for each. Which offers more spread?

parts.label: hedged yen yield of U.S. hotel (%)

rubric: Shows the hedged spread ratio equals the U.S. asset's spread over U.S. short rates
Concludes the Japanese hotel offers more spread before basis and diversification
Notes a negative basis makes the U.S. hedge worse for the yen investor

drills.solution: Hedged = 1.07 x 1.005/1.0425 - 1 = 3.156%. U.S. spread ratio = 1.07/1.0425 = 1.02638; Japan = 1.04/1.005 = 1.03483. The Japanese hotel offers more spread over its short rate.
common_mistakes: Using the long-rate differential as the hedge cost
drills.intuition: Under CIP a hedge moves the spread over short rates from one currency to another; it cannot create spread.
drills.takeaway: Compare (1+y)/(1+r) across markets, then adjust for the basis.
